questions.q: According to Dale Partridge, how do companies become dishonest?
a: Gradually, as growth pushes them off their early values
Immediately, because they are rotten from the start
Suddenly, when a new owner takes over the business
Naturally, because every founder eventually cuts corners
questions.why: Lesson 1 argues dishonesty is not built in at the start but grows slowly, and only when companies are pushed into it.

questions.q: Which part of McDonald's original promise slipped first as the chain grew?
a: Quality
Cleanliness
Service speed
Affordability
questions.why: Lesson 1 says quality was the first factor to fall off the company's roadmap as it had to serve more burgers faster.

questions.q: Why does the summary call trying to avoid transparency a fool's game?
a: Because the truth tends to surface no matter what
Because customers rarely check a company's claims
Because secrecy costs more than honest marketing
Because regulators punish hidden mistakes harshly
questions.why: Lesson 2 argues that even the biggest cover-up loses, since people can now check almost any claim within seconds.

questions.q: Which company does the summary hold up as an example of openness?
a: Buffer
Coca-Cola
McDonald's
Goldman Sachs
questions.why: Lesson 2 names Buffer as a great example of a company that shares its numbers with the world.

questions.q: What does the summary say consumers do with every dollar they spend?
a: Vote for the kind of business world they want
Support whichever brand advertises the most
Reward the companies with the lowest prices
Signal their income level to businesses
questions.why: Lesson 3 says we vote with every dollar, so half the responsibility for honest business rests with consumers.
